rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/config.rs: The lab accepts several kinds of test requests.
Parse valid requests and then supply missing, extra or unsupported arguments.
Select the requested task only for a supported argument list; reject the others before starting a workload.
SQLite can run one selected case or the full set on XFS.
Parse both forms, invalid selections and the default time limits.
Choose the requested XFS mode, reject malformed requests and apply the expected command and suite deadlines.
An operator can request a SQLite probe or an ext4 matrix run.
Parse complete and malformed requests and load their time limits.
Select only a supported workload and repetition. The probe and matrix must receive the deadlines for their respective modes.
The lab chooses deadlines before starting its workers.
Load several test modes with defaults and with environment overrides.
Use the limits for the selected mode. Invalid settings must not silently change how long a test may run.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/database_: A saved Linux device counter line includes data writes and requests to flush them.
Parse the line from the SQLite probe without running SQLite.
Report 204856 sectors written and 5558 flushes separately; the number of completed write requests is not a measure of data volume.
Device counters must describe transfers in complete storage blocks.
Pass truncated counters, aligned zero counts and inconsistent sector counts to the reader.
Read the valid counts and reject missing or misaligned data rather than publish a misleading transfer total.
A database observer needs the device number and accounting file to take a snapshot.
Supply a complete set of settings, then omit or invalidate individual values.
Read the intended device and file from valid settings and reject incomplete settings before collecting counters.
The observer has sample device and accounting counters at a known point in a database run.
Convert the snapshot to JSON and read back its fields.
Preserve the measurement phase, connection identity and counters so a report can associate them with the right event.
A prior run already wrote a file of evidence.
Ask the evidence writer to create another file at the same path.
Creation must fail and the file must still contain the original text. A later run must not erase the earlier observation.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/ext4/comm: The lab launches child commands and records their output.
Run one command that fails and another that exceeds its deadline.
Keep the command output in both cases, report the appropriate error and leave no managed child waiting for cleanup.
A suite has used up its time before the next command starts.
Ask the lab to start another command after the deadline.
Return a timeout without starting a child or advancing the command number.
A worker can receive explicit observer settings and may inherit unrelated variables from the parent.
Build its isolated environment and inspect which variables remain visible.
Keep the selected observer values; do not pass through unrelated secrets or inherited defaults that would change the test.
The lab owns a temporary directory and a backing image inside it.
Add an unexpected entry before asking the lab to clean up.
Refuse cleanup without deleting the backing image. Once the unexpected entry is removed, normal cleanup may finish.
A filesystem run needs a private directory owned by its user.
Check directory ownership, access permissions and a missing path before starting work.
Accept the existing private directory for its owner. Reject unsafe or missing directories rather than creating or using them implicitly.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/ext4/life: The SQLite lab formats its backing storage before measuring a database workload.
Inspect the format worker request and its accounting settings.
The worker must receive the specified accounting file so costs of formatting are associated with the intended run.
A daemon announces which device is ready with a line of text.
Parse a valid device announcement, unrelated paths and messages with extra output.
Accept just the canonical numbered device path. Do not let an unrelated device or an ambiguous message become the test target.
The filesystem acceptance plan orders device startup, mounts, checks and restart.
Walk the proposed sequence and track whether the device is running and mounted at each step.
All four filesystem checks must occur while unmounted. The plan must include the clean restart and three repetitions.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/ext4/requ: A sample request log contains reads with extra flags, writes, flushes and cancellations at shutdown.
Count completed operations and then introduce an unknown operation or a flush transferring data.
Exclude cancelled reads, retain valid hinted requests and reject inconsistent records instead of adding them to the totals.
The request log can include releases of unused disk ranges as well as data writes.
Validate the ranges and compare the transferred sectors with the device counters; try inconsistent reports.
Accept consistent totals and reject invalid range or sector information. A space release is not evidence that new client data was written.
A request report ends with a completeness record and counts for the operations it saw.
Give the reader inconsistent or incomplete records.
Reject the report rather than treat partial totals or contradictory discovery counts as a complete account of the run.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/ext4/sqli: An ARM host may provide numbered processor fields but no marketing model name.
Parse sample processor and memory information, including malformed fields.
Record the reported ARM identifiers and reject invalid data instead of guessing a CPU name.
A hardware description should identify the machine rather than its momentary load.
Parse sample processor and memory files, then try missing processor data and an invalid memory total.
Report stable hardware properties. Do not substitute free memory or current frequency for machine identity.
SQLite qualification combines workloads, database settings and repetitions.
Expand the complete schedule and count distinct entries without running any database.
Produce 87 distinct runs from 29 workload and settings combinations. No repeated entry may stand in for a missing one.
A user wants one member of the SQLite qualification schedule.
Try supported workload, settings and repetition combinations as well as unsupported ones.
Select a run only if it belongs to the published matrix; reject invalid combinations before creating a database.
A SQLite speed test prints separate lines for its main subtests.
Read sample output with the expected subtests, missing data and timing values too small to measure.
Require the full set of 32 subtests and retain the verification hash. Do not publish a zero measurement as a useful performance estimate.
A short key-value workload can finish within one tick of the tool’s clock.
Parse sample output reporting zero elapsed time and an infinite rate.
Keep the raw values for diagnosis but mark the derived measurements unavailable instead of presenting impossible throughput.
A SQLite worker can return an error or exceed its deadline.
Convert both errors into the JSON record used by the report.
Retain the distinction between failure and timeout, along with the diagnostic message, so an incomplete run cannot look successful.
The summarizer expects a result for a particular SQLite workload and filesystem.
Validate an XFS result against its intended selection, then against mismatched selections.
Accept the matching result only. An XFS run cannot satisfy an ext4 requirement.
The selected SQLite suite times out before all planned work starts.
Generate the partial summary from the selection and attempt counters.
Report timeout, retain the selected count and show only actual attempts. Do not count the remaining work as passed.
A database workload reports throughput as a decimal value.
Read the supplied rates into the summary and serialize the resulting numbers.
Preserve the reported values without rounding them to a different throughput or recomputing them from unrelated timings.
The SQLite lab accepts the complete matrix or an explicit single-case selection.
Check the expected set for the full list, a partial list and one selected run.
Accept the complete matrix and the single-run mode. Do not silently accept a truncated matrix as full qualification.
The lab selects one SQLite case from the full matrix and starts an attempt.
Record the attempted run and its failure, then read the saved manifest.
Distinguish 87 planned from one selected, one attempted and one failed. Save the failed case identity and leave no temporary manifest.
A SQLite run is identified by its workload, settings and repetition.
Generate the identity for the main speed test with full synchronous writes in write-ahead-log mode, repetition two.
Produce the stable name that includes all three parts, so evidence for different runs stays separate.
A database process reports elapsed time and paired snapshots of the device counters.
Parse a complete sample including time spent taking snapshots and closing the database.
Preserve the separate durations and differences; snapshot collection must not disappear into the reported workload time.
The SQLite speed test runs with a rollback journal instead of a write-ahead log.
Read telemetry for this profile without requiring generator activity or automatic checkpoints.
Accept the workload connection and recorded final checkpoint; do not impose write-ahead-log checkpoint requirements on this profile.
A long SQLite write-ahead-log workload exercises automatic copying of log data into the database.
Vary which connection reports the checkpoints and which workload is selected.
Require the qualifying checkpoints on the selected workload connection only for the case that promises to exercise them.
SQLite telemetry can include results from more than one database connection.
Give the reader a report with an explicit failure on a connection.
Reject the report even if a different connection appears healthy. A successful connection must not conceal another connection’s error.
A reference database run measures the process without collecting storage snapshots.
Read samples with and without process timing and device snapshots.
Require the process measurement, but reject snapshots in this mode rather than confuse reference timing with storage-instrumented timing.
The telemetry reader pairs measurements taken at different stages of a database run.
Remove or duplicate records and supply decreasing counters or invalid snapshot data.
Reject these reports. An incomplete or impossible measurement pair must not become a published difference.
The SQLite harness builds requests for several durability profiles.
Inspect the tool arguments and settings chosen for each profile.
Select the intended transaction and journal behavior without adding an option that changes the data-access method. This checks command construction, not database durability.
The database matrix includes speed tests and key-value workloads with different access patterns.
Build the tool requests and inspect their program, order, size and transaction settings.
Use the correct tool and arguments for each workload; a read case must not silently become an update.
The reporting code has a result for a selected SQLite filesystem run.
Build the structured result and inspect its schema, labels and scope.
Identify it as a versioned SQLite result for the selected filesystem and matrix rather than an unqualified database measurement.
SQLite may create temporary files or resolve relative paths from its working directory.
Inspect database worker requests before running them.
Set the intended temporary directory and database parent explicitly, so auxiliary files cannot escape into the caller’s working directory.
The lab validates a database by opening it without writing and comparing its output.
Inspect the validation request and try malformed rows alongside a valid digest.
Use the prescribed read-only invocation and accept only the expected validation output, not arbitrary text that happens to contain a checksum.
Device and engine counters are sampled before and after database activity.
Subtract the earlier snapshot from the later one, then swap their order.
Report exact differences for reads, flushes and backing writes. Reject decreasing counters rather than turn a reset into a large transfer.
Database timing includes workload execution, draining pending writes and the parent process envelope.
Compute reported durations from sample timings and then provide an inconsistent timing.
Use the process’s own measurements for the workload headline, report the parent elapsed time separately and reject impossible intervals.
The filesystem lab caps cumulative bytes written through its storage daemon.
Construct daemon and non-daemon requests and inspect their environment.
Pass the write-budget file only to the daemon. Other tools must not receive the path for charging the 512 MiB budget.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/ext4/work: The filesystem workload creates a known set of files in a temporary directory.
Verify the initial contents, try populating again and alter the stored files.
Reject a repeated population or a mismatch during verification. Finding the expected filename alone is not enough to show its contents survived.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/filesyste: The lab supports formatting and checking both ext4 and XFS.
Inspect the requests it builds for each filesystem without formatting any disk.
Use each filesystem’s own formatter with its intended defaults and request a read-only check rather than repairing the image during verification.
The filesystem worker uses a restricted helper to mount and unmount its test volume.
Select ext4 and XFS in turn and inspect helper actions and worker requests.
Choose the matching filesystem-specific action for both mount and unmount instead of using the ext4 helper for an XFS run.
A sample Linux mount table contains information about the options actually in effect.
Look up the mount identified by the recorded mount number and try a missing number.
Return the observed options for that mount only; do not infer them from the requested options or a different mount.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/main.rs::: The process supervisor starts a short-lived test child.
Wait for the child to exit normally within its deadline.
Report a successful exit rather than a timeout. No storage engine or filesystem is required for this check.
The process supervisor starts a child that deliberately stays alive.
Give the process less time than it needs to finish.
Return a timeout rather than reporting success or waiting indefinitely.
A managed child is still running and has a recorded process identifier.
Check that it is live, then explicitly request termination and wait for it.
Identify termination by the requested signal and collect the exit status instead of leaving a child behind.
The supervisor owns a running child process.
Send the unconditional kill signal and collect the exit status.
Report that exact signal. An arbitrary unsuccessful exit would not prove that the requested kill occurred.
A managed child is still alive when its owner releases the handle.
Drop the handle without explicitly waiting for a normal exit.
The supervisor must reap the process as part of cleanup rather than leave it alive or waiting for its parent.
A parent fixture starts another child in the same process group and reports its identity.
Let the supervising command exceed its time limit after the descendant starts.
Report a timeout and remove the descendant too. Killing only the immediately supervised parent is not sufficient.
The supervisor needs a child that finishes normally.
Launch this empty fixture as its child process; it performs no storage operations.
It should exit successfully. The separate supervisor test checks how the parent reports that exit.
A timeout test needs a process that outlives the deadline.
When selected as a child, pause for 60 seconds; otherwise return immediately.
The parent should be able to exercise its timeout path. Running this helper alone does not demonstrate that cleanup worked.
The timeout test needs a parent and a grandchild in one process group.
When selected as the fixture parent, start the leaf child and wait for its readiness file.
The leaf must signal readiness before the deadline, giving the outer supervisor a known descendant to clean up.
A supervisor test needs to identify the grandchild before forcing a timeout.
When selected as the leaf, write the process identifier to the readiness file and sleep.
The outer test can then check whether this specific descendant survived cleanup. Without the fixture setting the helper returns immediately.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/suite.rs:: The suite runner receives a text listing of test cases and other output.
Parse the listing before scheduling cases.
Include entries marked as tests and exclude unrelated lines so summaries or other items do not become invented test runs.
The suite displays elapsed durations and classifies slow tests.
Format a sample interval and classify sample durations against the timing thresholds.
Use the expected precision and timing category. This checks presentation, not the speed of a storage workload.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/ublk.rs::: A daemon supplies a numbered Linux block-device path.
Try a valid path for device 42 and a range of noncanonical strings.
Recover the exact number and path from the valid name and reject alternatives rather than opening an unintended target.
The live I/O plan has a small backing file and a larger client-visible volume.
Compute the expected storage geometry without creating a device.
Distinguish the 322 backing blocks from the 4 MiB logical volume and preserve the 128 KiB segment size.
A test supplies a simulated Linux device directory and kernel attribute files.
Check device identity, capacity and the major and minor numbers; alter or omit identifying information.
Accept matching geometry and reject inconsistent identity rather than attaching a workload to the wrong device.
Filesystem acceptance uses a different volume size from the small direct-I/O workload.
Validate sample kernel geometry using the appropriate and inappropriate expected sizes.
Require the correct capacity for the selected test; an image sized for another workload must not pass this check.
The test creates a private directory and records its identity and ownership marker.
Attempt cleanup after changing the evidence of ownership, then restore safe conditions.
Refuse removal when ownership cannot be proved and remove only the original, marked directory.
The I/O tool normally can save verification state in its current directory.
Build the request for the test target and inspect its options.
Disable saving verification state there. Running a verification workload must not leave a state file among the caller’s unrelated files.
The lab constructs several I/O jobs for a nonexistent target.
Ask the installed workload tool to parse the generated job options without running the workload.
The tool must accept the command shapes. This tests compatibility with its parser, not successful reads or writes on a device.
rust/src/bin/block-storage-lab/ublk_fio/: The device acceptance plan includes ordinary writes and a deliberate exhaustion scenario.
Count the scenarios, repetitions and planned writes and compare them with the test image capacity.
Schedule eight scenarios three times each. The exhaustion case must attempt more writes than fit in the log.
Some live-device scenarios restart or kill the daemon between writing data and checking it.
Inspect the planned transitions for those scenarios.
The plan must explicitly request the intended restart or kill and the required verification steps, not merely finish after writing.
The lab creates output names for multiple commands in one owned directory.
Ask the name allocator for successive outputs, including separate output and error files.
Give each operation its intended distinct names. Later commands must not overwrite evidence from earlier operations.
The daemon log contains several lines of statistics.
Extract counters by exact name from the last structured entry and try unmatched fields.
Read the final reported values, not an earlier value or a field whose name only ends in the requested text.
The lab checks the I/O tool’s structured output for the disk-full scenario.
Parse a sample job result and try missing jobs or malformed numeric fields.
Extract the error code and byte count from the required fields; reject unusable data rather than infer successful exhaustion.
The device workload has repeatable random writes and bounded transfer sizes.
Inspect the arguments for each generated I/O request, including the wraparound passes.
Preserve the specified seed, direct-I/O setting and transfer budget for the scenario; this does not run the workload itself.
The device harness constructs requests for formatting and for bounded I/O jobs.
Inspect the executable, working directory, test target and workload arguments without starting the device.
Use the owned directory and fixed workload sizes so these requests cannot expand into an unrestricted benchmark.
The format worker receives a new backing path for a volume whose geometry does not round to whole mebibytes.
Format it, inspect its size and volume description, then attempt to format the occupied path again.
Preserve the exact backing length and ten segments; refuse to replace the existing image.
The kernel control device is absent from the preflight check.
Supply the missing-path condition before attempting a workload.
Explain that the control node is missing and identify the operator action needed. Do not proceed as though device setup succeeded.
A file exists at the control path but is not the required type of device.
Run the preflight check on this incorrect node type.
Reject it with a diagnostic that distinguishes a wrong type from a missing path. A regular file is not a usable control device.
The control node exists but the test user lacks access.
Give the preflight check the observed node information and a permission error.
Return permission denied, describe the observations and identify the remedy. Do not report this as a storage-engine failure.
The control path has the expected character-device type and is accessible.
Give the preflight check those observations before any live-device workload starts.
Accept this prerequisite. Passing this check alone does not mean a block device was created or tested.
The lab owns a temporary backing file with the expected identity and length.
Validate it, shorten it to one byte and check the saved backing reference again.
Accept the intact file but reject it after the size change rather than running the workload on unexpected storage.
A child writes a readiness announcement while the test supplies fake device directories.
Let the readiness checker poll the announcement and matching kernel attributes.
Return device number seven once its identity is established. The fixture tests polling without creating a real kernel block device.
A readiness announcement identifies the expected device but access is initially denied.
Use a simulated access check that succeeds only after retries.
Verify identity before retrying access, then return the intended device when permission becomes available.
A readiness announcement exists, but the user cannot open the indicated device.
Keep returning permission denied until the readiness deadline.
Try more than once, then report a timeout with the pending permission problem. Do not mark the device ready.
A child can disappear before announcing its device or remain alive without announcing it.
Check readiness for an early exit and for a sleeping child.
Distinguish the unexpected exit from expiry of the deadline. Neither case supplies a ready device.
An I/O command writes a diagnostic to each output stream and exits unsuccessfully.
Let the harness record its output and process its exit status.
Keep both diagnostic messages before returning the status error so the cause remains available in the run evidence.
A controlled crash test owns a daemon child and needs proof of how it stopped.
Request an unconditional kill and inspect the recorded outcome.
Require the exact kill signal and clear the managed child after collecting it. A mere nonzero status does not establish this crash condition.
A fixture child exits unsuccessfully for a reason other than the requested kill.
Present that exit to the crash-test supervisor.
Reject it and explain that the expected kill signal was missing. An unrelated daemon failure cannot satisfy this crash test.
The harness must identify its device before deciding whether removal is safe.
Present simulated kernel observations for an active device, a stopped one, a replacement and a missing device.
Distinguish all four states; the same numeric device name alone does not prove ownership.
After a kill, kernel information can be briefly incomplete while the device stops.
Supply one partial identity check followed by a matching stopped device.
Wait and retry before permitting deletion. Only the complete, matching stopped identity is safe to remove.
The device identity stays uncertain after a kill.
Keep returning incomplete observations until the retry allowance runs out.
Return the last specific inspection error and preserve the resources. Do not delete a device whose identity has not been established.
A device now has a different identity from the one the lab recorded.
Supply the changed identity during removal after a kill.
Refuse deletion immediately and preserve the resources. Retrying until the number appears reusable would risk deleting someone else’s device.
Only part of the identifying device information exists under the simulated kernel paths.
Ask the harness to classify the device before cleanup.
Report that the identity is only partially present. Missing fields are not proof that the original device has disappeared.
Cleanup has the recorded identity of the test device.
Supply matching observations showing that the same device has stopped.
Allow removal of that recorded device and complete cleanup. This tests the decision to delete under controlled observations.
The cleanup routine knows which backing file and device belonged to the test.
Supply observations showing that the device identity has changed.
Refuse to delete the device and preserve its backing file rather than acting on the reused device number.
The cleanup routine cannot obtain a definite identity for the device.
Ask it to clean up with that ambiguity unresolved.
Return an error and leave the backing file intact. An inconclusive identity check must never authorize deletion.
A workload cannot satisfy its prerequisites.
Run the failing preflight against test-owned paths and inspect them afterwards.
Report the failure before creating evidence directories, temporary files or device resources. No cleanup of a partially started workload should be necessary.
The readiness test needs a daemon-like child but does not need a real device.
When enabled, write the path for device seven to the supplied readiness file and sleep.
The parent can poll a realistic announcement from a live process. Outside the fixture the helper does nothing.
The readiness supervisor needs a process that exits before producing an announcement.
Launch this empty child fixture, which exits without writing a device path.
The parent can test its early-exit handling. The empty child itself makes no storage assertion.
A supervisor test needs an exit that is neither success nor the requested kill signal.
When the fixture setting is present, exit with status 23.
The parent should observe an ordinary nonzero exit to distinguish it from death by signal. Otherwise the fixture returns normally.
The readiness supervisor needs a process that stays alive without identifying a device.
When enabled as a child, sleep for 60 seconds and write no announcement.
The parent can exercise its deadline while the child is still alive. The helper alone does not test a real device.
